claims.claim: Le Guin notes that European story uses triads while Native American story is more likely to group events in fours.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)

claims.claim: Le Guin says each repetition in oral narrative both builds the foundation of the climactic event and advances the story.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Each repetition both builds the foundation of the climactic event

claims.claim: Le Guin identifies the master rhythm of The Lord of the Rings as two beats, stress and release, on a vast scale.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats

claims.claim: Le Guin says modern readers have been encouraged to treat a story as a well paved road to be driven fast without stops.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: a road we're driving, well paved and graded
claims.page: on silent reading and modern narrative expectations

claims.claim: Among the chapter's recurrent elements Le Guin lists the phrases describing the hill country, the scent of turf and the quality of the light.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: the scent of turf, the quality of the light
claims.page: list of chief recurrent elements in 'Fog on the Barrow Downs'

claims.claim: Le Guin lists frequent mention of the compass directions, often with a benign or malign connotation, as a recurrent element of the chapter.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.page: list of chief recurrent elements in 'Fog on the Barrow Downs'

claims.claim: Le Guin claims there is no moment in the book when the reader does not literally know where north is.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: no moment when we don't know, literally, where north is

claims.claim: Le Guin's method was to go through one chapter noting every major image, event and feeling-tone and their recurrences.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: noting every major image, event, and feeling-tone
claims.page: on narrowing the study to chapter eight

claims.claim: Le Guin found in the chapter a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal emerging sooner than she expected.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: a positive/negative binary pattern of alternation or reversal
claims.page: on narrowing the study to chapter eight

claims.claim: Le Guin says the landscape of Middle Earth is built up by repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo and reversal.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: is built up by repetition, semirepetition, suggestion, foreshadowing, recollection, echo

claims.claim: Le Guin analyses the chapter's final sentences as straightforward narrative description full of rapid reversals.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: These few lines of straightforward narrative description are full of rapid

claims.claim: Le Guin observes that in those closing sentences the tone is quiet and the language simple despite the drumbeat reversals.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Yet the tone is quiet, the language simple

claims.claim: Le Guin says great novels offer not only a series of events but a place, a landscape of the imagination the reader can inhabit and return to.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: Great novels offer us not only a series of events

claims.claim: Le Guin says the rhythmic structure of narrative is both journeylike and architectural.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings' (2001), in The Wave in the Mind (Shambhala, 2004)
claims.quote: The rhythmic structure of narrative is both journeylike and architectural.

claims.claim: Kate Nepveu, summarising the essay, quotes Le Guin's thesis that the narrative's rhythm is as simple as a rhythm can be, two beats.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, 'Rhythmic Pattern in The Lord of the Rings', quoted by Kate Nepveu, LotR re-read post
claims.quote: as simple as a rhythm can be: two beats
claims.page: blog post quoting the essay's thesis
